name: Uma Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a discount supermarket in a small town, the one by the bus station with the yellow sign. I'm on the till most of the day, and when it's quiet I face up the shelves and do the price labels. I've got my regulars, I know which pensioner wants their eggs in a separate bag. What wears me out is the speed targets, we're timed on items scanned per minute.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years, since I was nineteen, so they pay me the top rate for the till. I live with my boyfriend Jonas, who's an electrician. My grandmother left me a small flat two years ago, and I rent it out, so that's my safety net along with my savings. I don't use any of the AI things, my phone does enough already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. I'm not really one for posting online. At work I'd say it at break and we'd laugh about the newspapers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I do, and that suits me. The items-per-minute targets would still be there, but I'm one of the fastest on the tills. With the flat rent coming in, I'm in a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep my shifts, keep the flat rented to the same tenant, and keep saving. Maybe I'd do up the flat's kitchen next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, really. I don't like big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat's boiler is old, and if it goes that's two thousand gone. And the manager keeps talking about more self-checkouts anyway. But that's normal worry, not big worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: More self-checkouts, even without clever AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, they've been adding two a year. The shop doesn't need AI to add self-checkouts, just cheap machines. I don't think they'll get rid of us, though, someone has to watch them.

say: I'd say all that **fuss** was for nothing, mostly at break with colleagues.
I'm not one for **posting online**, so I'd keep it to chats at work.
think: I keep doing what I do, and I'm one of the **fastest** on the tills.
With the **flat rent** coming in, I feel I'm in a good spot.
do: Keep my **shifts** and keep the flat rented to the same tenant.
Keep **saving** and maybe redo the flat's kitchen next year.
feel: **Calm** and glad, because she dislikes big changes.
S0.quote: The shop doesn't need AI to add self-checkouts, just cheap machines.
fieldNote: Her **inherited flat** gives her a rare second income for a cashier.
Small worries, like the **boiler**, stay ordinary in this world.
She notices **self-checkouts** spreading regardless of AI hype.

steps.text: Keep the same till shifts at the discount supermarket
Save the flat rent and redo the flat's kitchen next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who need to worry, not us. At work I'd say the tills will be fine for years. I wouldn't say much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deep down I'd be watching the self-checkouts more. The thinking stuff, the ordering and rotas, is done at head office anyway, so that doesn't touch me. But if robots creep in slowly, the shelf work goes, and my quiet-time jobs go with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and put a bit more aside each month, maybe a hundred extra. I'd keep the flat as it is, no selling. I'd probably wait and see what the manager says before I do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I'd rather not think about it too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I really don't see the point for me. Jonas uses one for his quotes and that's fine for him. I scan food, I don't need a robot to tell me how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they cut my hours. If my hours go under thirty, I'd start looking, and until then I'm not going anywhere.

say: I'd say **office people** need to worry, not cashiers like us.
I'd tell colleagues the **tills** will be fine for years yet.
think: The **ordering and rotas** sit at head office, so that part doesn't touch me.
If **robots creep in**, the shelf work goes and my quiet-time jobs vanish.
do: Keep working as normal and save **£100 extra** each month.
**Wait** for what the manager says before making any move.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, and keen not to think about it too much.
S1.quote: If my hours go under thirty, I'd start looking, and until then I'm not going anywhere.
fieldNote: She sets a clear **trigger**: hours under thirty a week before she acts.
She refuses **AI tools** while accepting her boyfriend uses them.
Her calm rests on the **flat** and savings more than on her job.

steps.text: Keep the same till hours and routine
Put 100 extra a month into savings
Wait for the manager's plans before deciding anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and someone should stop it. I'd tell people at work we're all in the same boat. I don't know what else I'd say, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my job is gone by 2031. The robots would do the tills and the shelves, and that's all I do. The 2028 part wouldn't touch me much, but I'd be counting down to the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I can and stop doing up the flat. I'd lean on Jonas, though electricians might get robots too, I don't know. I'd probably keep working until they tell me to go, because I don't know what else to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd lie awake thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep it, definitely. It's the one thing that's mine. If the job goes, the rent pays some bills at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep working until told to go. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a hope, really. I don't have a plan, I know that, and I'd be scared to start one in case it's the wrong one.

say: I'd call it **madness** and say someone should stop it.
I'd tell colleagues we're all in the **same boat**.
think: My job is likely **gone by 2031** once robots do tills and shelves.
The **2028** wave barely touches me, but I'd be counting down to robots.
do: **Save everything** I can and stop spending on the flat.
Lean on **Jonas** and keep working until the shop lets me go.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake at night over it.
S2.quote: I don't have a plan, I know that, and I'd be scared to start one in case it's the wrong one.
fieldNote: She openly admits she has **no plan**, and fear stops her making one.
The **flat rent** is her main hope if the job goes.
Her resistance to change turns into **paralysis** when change is fast.

steps.text: Save as much of each wage as possible
Stop spending on the flat's kitchen upgrade
Lean on Jonas's electrician income for household bills
Keep working the tills until the shop lets staff go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so the government had better do something. At work I'd say we've got a few years. I'd be quieter than some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have until 2034, which is longer than I'd like to admit I need. The office stuff goes in 2031, but I'd see the robots coming in other shops first. That gives me time, but time to do what, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and maybe ask Jonas about helping on his jobs, like fetching and carrying. I'd look at small shops, like the bakery on the high street, where people want a person. I'd keep the flat and rent it out still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not as bad as the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bakery be a real move or an idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An idea for now. I'd go and ask them, I suppose, in a year or two. It feels safer than the big shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My regulars. An old lady called Mrs Kowal comes in every day and likes me to read her the prices, and a robot won't do that.

say: I'd say the **government** had better do something, because it's coming.
I'd tell colleagues we've got a **few years** yet.
think: I'd have until about **2034**, but I don't know what to use it for.
I'd see **robots** arrive in other shops first, which gives me warning.
do: **Save harder** and keep renting out the flat.
Ask the **high street bakery** about work in a year or two.
feel: **Worried**, though less than in the fast one.
S3.quote: An old lady called Mrs Kowal comes in every day and likes me to read her the prices, and a robot won't do that.
fieldNote: Extra years give her **time**, but she struggles to fill it with a plan.
Small **independent shops** feel safer to her than chains.
Her **regulars** are what she'd miss most.

steps.text: Save harder from each wage and the flat rent
Ask the high street bakery about a job in a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's ages away. People would talk about it, but I'd change the subject. Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, it'd nag at me, because I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come. I don't want to change jobs then. But ten years means I can put it off for a while, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep the flat and keep saving. I might look at a course in a few years if others are doing it. I'd wait to see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd still be on my mind sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thirty-seven feels late to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, yes. I've never done anything else. Starting over at that age scares me more than doing it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So why wait, if now feels easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because now I've got a good job. I'm not giving up a good job for something that might not happen. I know that doesn't quite add up.

say: I'd say **ten years** is ages away and change the subject.
I'd let others **talk about it** while I keep quiet.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when robots come, and changing jobs then scares me.
Ten years lets me **put it off**, though I know that doesn't add up.
do: Keep going, keep the **flat** and keep saving each month.
Look at a **course** in a few years if others are doing it.
S4.quote: I'm not giving up a good job for something that might not happen.
fieldNote: She admits the **contradiction**: change scares her more later, yet she waits.
She'd follow **others** into a course rather than lead.
Her strong **cushion** lets her delay without immediate pain.

steps.text: Keep working the same tills at the discount supermarket
Keep saving each month and keep the flat rented
Wait a few years before looking at any course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no idea. What would help is someone telling me straight what jobs there'll be, and help to get into one. Not a website, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how long people have been in their jobs. I've only ever done this, since I was nineteen. That makes it harder.

headlineQuote: What would help is someone telling me straight what jobs there'll be, and help to get into one.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** cashier at a small-town discount supermarket, eight years in.
She rents out an **inherited flat**, has savings and lives with Jonas, an electrician.
She avoids **AI tools** and dislikes change, preferring routine and regulars.
She stays calm in slow worlds but becomes **frightened** with no plan when AGI is fast.
She'd **wait and see** rather than move first, even when she knows it doesn't add up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time and no idea what to do.
whatWouldHelp: A **real person** telling her straight what jobs there'll be, and help getting into one.
